title: What an API Is and What It's For
summary: Learn what an API is, what people build with one, what a server really is, and how an API's requests and responses are shaped.
intro: Every app you use leans on APIs: the weather on your phone, the map in a page, the card form in a shop. When one of them breaks, the error you see is often an API's answer, passed along. This lesson sets up the words the rest of the course relies on: what an API is and why teams build them, who calls APIs and what for, what a server really is, how requests and responses carry an API's data, and what an API is made of. Along the way you'll call a real public API, and meet the endpoints of Roombook, the API you'll build.

steps.title: Programs that talk to programs
steps.body:
Two programs can only work together if they agree on how to talk. An API is that agreement, and everything you build in this course is one, so it's worth getting the idea exactly right.

## An API is a contract

An **API**, short for application programming interface, is the set of requests a program accepts and the answers it promises for each one. The web course met two kinds: the functions a browser offers your JavaScript, and addresses on a server that answer with data. Both are a program saying: ask me this way, and you'll get this back.

Think of a restaurant's menu. It lists what you can order and what you'll get, and it hides the kitchen. The kitchen can buy a new stove or change cooks, and nobody at the tables notices, as long as the dishes still match the menu. That's why people call an API a **contract**: both sides rely on it, and either side can change everything else.

Roombook's contract says things like this: send `GET /v1/rooms/1` and you get room 1 as JSON, with its name and how many people it seats. Ask for a room that doesn't exist and you get a 404, with an error in a format you can read the same way every time.

## Clients and servers

Recall the two roles from the web course. The **client** is the program that asks, and the **server** is the program that answers. With an API, the client is usually code: a page's JavaScript, a phone app, another company's server. One program can play both roles. Roombook is a server to the phone app, and a client of the email service it asks to send booking confirmations.

Because the two sides only meet at the contract, each can change on its own. You can rewrite Roombook's insides, move its data to a new database, or run it on ten computers, and the phone app never knows. The flip side: once clients depend on the contract, changing it can break them, which is why a later lesson covers changing an API safely.

## Why teams build APIs

```diagram what-apis-are-one-api
Four kinds of clients, one API, and only the API touches the database.
```

The diagram shows why almost every company with an app has an API. The website, the phone app, a partner's program, and the screens by each room's door all ask the same API, and only the API talks to the database. So the rules, like no double bookings, live in one place and protect the data from every client at once. Without the API, every client would need the database's password, and every one would have to enforce every rule itself, the same way, forever.

## Library APIs and web APIs

The word API is older than the web. A **library API** is the functions and types a library offers your code inside the same program. A **web API** is offered by another program, over the network, through HTTP. Here's one of each in Python:

```python
import json
from datetime import date
from urllib.request import urlopen

day = date.fromisoformat("2026-10-05")
print(day.strftime("%A"))

with urlopen("https://api.github.com/repos/fastapi/fastapi") as response:
    repo = json.load(response)
print(repo["stargazers_count"])
```

`date.fromisoformat` and `strftime` are a library API, from Python's standard library. `urlopen`, from the standard library too, sends a request to GitHub's web API and waits for the answer to cross the network. Later lessons use httpx2, a friendlier library for the same job.

The two look alike, but they behave very differently. A library call takes a few billionths of a second, and it can't fail because a network did. A web API call takes from a few milliseconds to several seconds, it can fail in ways a library call never does, like no connection, a timeout, or an error from the server, and its answer arrives as text that you have to parse and check. Much of this course is about those differences: checking what arrives, giving up in time, and trying again safely.

This course is about web APIs, so from here on, API means a web API.

examples.title: The same data, for people and for programs
examples.prompt: GitHub shows the FastAPI project to people at `github.com/fastapi/fastapi`, and its API serves the same facts to programs. On a Mac or Linux, ask for them with curl, and keep four lines of the answer with grep.
examples.output:
"full_name": "fastapi/fastapi",
  "description": "FastAPI framework, high performance, easy to learn, fast to code, ready for production",
  "stargazers_count": 105001,
  "language": "Python",
examples.explanation: The whole answer is JSON, about a hundred lines of it, and grep keeps four. `full_name` and `description` are the same words you'd see at the top of the project's page, and `stargazers_count` is how many people starred it. The page and the API share one set of data. The page wraps it in HTML for people to read, and the API sends it bare, for programs to use. Sites that show a project's stars, and bots that answer in its issues, are all clients of this API. Run it later and the star count will have moved, since the API answers with the data as it is right now. GitHub lets you ask 60 times an hour without signing in, a limit you'll see in its headers at the end of this lesson.

steps.title: What people use APIs for
steps.body:
Knowing who calls APIs, and why, tells you what yours has to get right. A public API lives or dies by its docs, an internal one by its speed, and a phone app's by how few requests each screen needs.

## Public APIs

Some companies sell an API as their product. **Stripe** takes card payments for millions of shops through one, **Google Maps** draws maps and finds routes, **Twilio** sends text messages, and AI companies answer questions through theirs. Other public APIs come free with a product, like GitHub's, which you just called. A public API has thousands of clients its makers will never meet, so it needs clear docs, keys to know who's calling, limits on how much each may ask, and a promise not to break for years.

## Partner APIs

A **partner API** is shared with a few other companies under an agreement. An airline sells seats through travel sites, a shop sends orders to its delivery company, and a university's timetable system could tell Roombook which rooms are taken by classes. There are fewer clients, but each one is a business that depends on you.

## Internal APIs

Most API calls in the world happen inside one company. A large backend is often split into smaller programs called **services**, each owning one job, like payments, search, or email, and they talk to each other through their APIs. Nobody outside sees these, so they're tuned for speed and change more freely. The Distributed Systems section covers how such systems hold together.

## Backends for web and phone apps

The most common API of all is the one behind a company's own website and phone app, and that's what Roombook is. When one screen needs data from many places, teams sometimes build a **backend for frontend**, or **BFF**: an API made for one client's screens, which gathers everything a screen needs into one response. A phone on a weak signal pays for every extra request, so phone apps gain the most.

## Integrations, automation, and devices

- **Integrations** connect tools. When a booking is confirmed, add it to the student's calendar. When a form is sent, open a support ticket. Services like Zapier exist to wire APIs together this way.
- **Automation** is code that calls APIs with no person involved, like a nightly script that emails tomorrow's bookings to each library.
- **CLIs**, command-line interfaces, are programs you run in a terminal, and many are API clients. `gh`, GitHub's CLI, calls the API you just used.
- **IoT**, the Internet of Things, means devices that use the internet, like thermostats, sensors, and card readers. Each one is a client.

## Roombook's callers

Roombook has a device of its own: a small screen beside each room's door that shows the day's bookings. Nobody signs in to it, so it proves who it is with an **API key**, a long secret string that identifies a program rather than a person. It asks for the schedule every minute, all day, so a thousand screens send a thousand nearly identical requests a minute, which is exactly the load that caching is for. Here are all of Roombook's callers, and how each proves who it is:

| Caller | Who's behind it | How it proves who it is |
|---|---|---|
| The website | a student in a browser | a session cookie |
| The phone app | a student on a phone | a token in a header |
| Scripts | a student's own code | a token in a header |
| Door screens | a device, with no person | an API key |
| Staff sign-in | library staff | their university account |

The Authentication and Authorization section builds each of these, and the Distributed Systems section adds the cache the door screens need.

steps.title: What a server is
steps.body:
Server sounds like special hardware in a cold room. It's much simpler than that, and knowing what it really is tells you where to look when yours won't answer.

## Any computer running your code

The web course used the word for the program that answers and for the computer it runs on. In this course, a **server** is any computer running your code and listening for requests. Your laptop becomes one as soon as you start Roombook on it. In production, the server is usually a computer in a **data center**, a building full of computers with fast network links and backup power, rented from a company like Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud, or Microsoft Azure. Renting computers this way, by the hour, is what people mean by **the cloud**.

## A process listening on a port

A program that's running is called a **process**, and your operating system gives each one a number, its PID, which the web course used to find what held a port. A server is a process that has asked the operating system to **listen** on a port: to hand it every connection that arrives for that number. When you run `fastapi dev`, it starts **Uvicorn**, the server program FastAPI runs on, which asks to listen on port 8000 and calls your code for each request.

Here's the whole path from a name to your code:

```diagram what-apis-are-reaching-handler
DNS finds the computer, the port finds the process, and the method and path find the handler.
```

In step 1, the client asks DNS for the name's IP address, as in the web course. In step 2, it connects to that address and port, and the operating system hands the connection to the process listening there: Roombook. In step 3, FastAPI reads the request, and its **router**, the part that matches each request's method and path to your code, picks a **handler**, the function you wrote for that endpoint. In step 4, the handler runs, and its answer goes back the same way. Each step fails in its own way. A name with no DNS record fails at step 1, a server that's stopped fails at step 2 with connection refused, and a path with no handler reaches the server and gets a 404.

## Who can reach it

Recall from the web course that a server picks which of its computer's addresses it listens on:

- `127.0.0.1`, or localhost, means only programs on the same computer can connect. It's what you want while you build, and the small server from the Start Here lesson uses it.
- `0.0.0.0` means every address the computer has. On a real server, or inside a **container**, which packs your app with everything it needs so it runs the same on any computer, the requests come from outside, so the API has to listen on all of them.
- A **public IP address** is one the whole internet can reach. Real APIs rarely put themselves on one directly. A **load balancer** or a **reverse proxy**, a server that takes every request first and passes it on, sits in front, and DNS points the API's name at it. The Distributed Systems section covers why.

## Where servers run

Your code can run in several kinds of places, and each takes a different share of the work off your hands:

| Option | What it is | What you look after | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your own computer | your laptop, running the API | everything | building and trying things |
| A virtual machine | a slice of a big computer in a data center, acting like a whole computer of its own | the operating system and everything on it | full control |
| A container platform | a service that runs your app packed as a container | the container and its settings | most new APIs |
| A platform as a service | a service you hand your code to, which builds and runs it | your code and settings | small teams with no time for servers |
| Serverless functions | a service that runs your handlers only when requests come in | the handlers | spiky traffic and small jobs |

The Production section packs Roombook into a container. **Serverless** doesn't mean there's no server. It means you never see one: the provider starts your code when a request arrives, and stops it when traffic dies down. FastAPI runs well on all of them.

examples.title: Which process is the server
examples.prompt: With the small server from the Start Here lesson running in one terminal, ask your computer from a second one which process listens on port 8000. On a Mac or Linux, `lsof` lists it, and `awk` keeps three of its columns.
examples.explanation: `-iTCP:8000` asks about TCP port 8000, `-sTCP:LISTEN` keeps only processes listening there, and `-nP` prints numbers instead of names. Under the column names come two lines, both `Python`. `fastapi dev` starts two processes: the first watches your files, and the second is the server, which the first restarts each time you save a change. The first opens the port and hands it to the second, so both show up. The numbers are their PIDs, which will be different on your computer. `127.0.0.1:8000` is the address and port: loopback only, so nothing outside your computer can connect. Stop the server and run the command again, and it prints nothing. It's the same check you'd make when a server won't start because the address is already in use.

steps.title: Requests and responses, for an API
steps.body:
Everything an API says travels as HTTP, the requests and responses you read in the web course. This part recalls their shape, and adds what changes when the client is a program and the body is data.

## The shape, recalled

A request is a request line (a method, a path, and the HTTP version), then headers, a blank line, and sometimes a body. A response is a status line (the version, a status code, and usually a few words), then headers, a blank line, and a body. Here's a client asking Roombook to book a room:

```diagram what-apis-are-exchange
A request and its response share one shape. In an API, both bodies are JSON.
```

## What's different with an API

- **Both bodies are JSON.** A browser mostly sends form fields and gets HTML back. An API client sends JSON and gets JSON back, so both messages carry `Content-Type: application/json`, and the client says what it can read with `Accept`.
- **Every method gets used.** A browser sends GET for pages and POST for forms. API clients use all the methods from the web course: GET to read, POST to create, PUT and PATCH to change, and DELETE to remove. The Handling Requests section covers each one.
- **The status code is the first thing a program reads.** A person can read an error page and work out what happened. A program can't, so the code has to be exactly right. Recall the classes: 2xx means it worked, 3xx means look elsewhere or use your copy, 4xx means the client has to change its request, and 5xx means the server failed, so the client may try again later.
- **Headers carry the rest.** `Authorization` carries the caller's credentials, the proof of who they are. `Location`, in the diagram, says where the new booking now lives. Later lessons add more, like `ETag` and `Retry-After`.

## Stateless, so every request says who it is

Recall that HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone, and the server doesn't remember the one before. For an API, that means every request carries everything the server needs to answer it, credentials included, in a cookie or an `Authorization` header. It sounds wasteful, but it's what lets any one of ten copies of Roombook answer any request, which the Distributed Systems section relies on.

## HTTPS and HTTP versions

Every real API uses HTTPS, since every request carries credentials, and anyone along the way could read them from plain HTTP. On your own computer, plain `http://localhost` is fine, because the messages never leave it.

HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3 change how messages travel, not what they say. Your handler sees the same method, path, headers, and body in all three. The version is agreed between the client and whatever answers first, which in production is usually the load balancer in front of your API. On your own computer, curl and FastAPI use HTTP/1.1.

examples.title: Booking a room, as curl sees it
examples.prompt: Ask Roombook, on port 8000, to book room 1. `--json` sends the text after it as a JSON body in a POST, and `-v` prints everything curl sends and receives. This is Roombook as it will be once the Handling Requests section is done.

> POST /v1/bookings HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:8000
> User-Agent: curl/8.7.1
> Content-Type: application/json
> Accept: application/json
> Content-Length: 133
>
* upload completely sent off: 133 bytes
< HTTP/1.1 201 Created
< date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 22:55:18 GMT
< server: uvicorn
< location: /v1/bookings/1001
< content-length: 213
< content-type: application/json
<

{"id":1001,"roomId":1,"userId":1,"startsAt":"2026-10-05T14:00:00Z","endsAt":"2026-10-05T15:30:00Z","attendees":3,"note":"Algorithms study group","status":"confirmed","version":1,"createdAt":"2026-10-01T09:00:00Z"}
examples.explanation: The lines starting with `*` are curl's notes, as in the web course. The lines starting with `>` are the request: `--json` chose POST and added `Content-Type: application/json` and `Accept: application/json` for you. `Content-Length: 133` counts the JSON's bytes, and curl notes when it has sent them, without printing the body itself. The lines starting with `<` are the response. `201 Created` means a new thing exists now, and `location` says where, so a client could `GET /v1/bookings/1001` next. The body is the new booking, with what the server added: its `id`, the `userId` of whoever booked, a `status`, and when it was made. It prints after curl's last note only because curl holds back a line of the body until it ends, and this body has no line break at the end. The real endpoint also needs to know who's booking, which the Authentication and Authorization section adds.

steps.title: What an API is made of
steps.body:
Clients never see your code. All they see is the API's surface: its addresses, what each one accepts and returns, how it fails, and the rules around it. Getting that surface right is most of what designing an API means.

## Endpoints, resources, and representations

An **endpoint** is one method and one path pattern that the API answers, like `GET /v1/rooms/{roomId}`. The `{roomId}` is a **path parameter**: a placeholder that each request fills in, like the 3 in `/v1/rooms/3`. A **resource** is a thing the API lets clients work with: a room, a booking, the list of bookings, or room 3's free times on a given day. A **representation** is a resource written down for one response, in JSON here. The resource itself stays on the server, and clients only ever get copies, which is why a representation can leave out fields the server keeps to itself.

Here's one request's address, piece by piece:

```diagram what-apis-are-url-anatomy
The method and the path pattern make the endpoint. The values in the path and query pick the resource.
```

The scheme and the host are the same pieces as in the web course, and APIs often get a host name of their own, like `api.roombook.example`, apart from the website's. `/v1` is the API's version, which you'll meet again below. `/rooms` names a **collection**, all the rooms, and `/3` picks one item in it. `/availability` is a **sub-resource**, something that belongs to room 3. The query string, `?date=2026-10-05`, carries options, here which day. The method, GET, says what to do with it all.

## Inputs and outputs

For every endpoint, the contract says what goes in and what comes out:

- **In:** path parameters, query parameters, headers, and maybe a JSON body, each with a type and the values it allows.
- **Out, on success:** the status code and the shape of the body. Roombook's lists, for example, always come back as `{"items": [...], "nextCursor": ...}`.
- **Out, on failure:** a status code, and a body that says what went wrong.

## One error format

If every endpoint reported errors its own way, every client would need code for each one. So a good API answers every error in one shape. Roombook uses **Problem Details**, a standard numbered RFC 9457. An **RFC** is one of the documents published by the IETF, the group that writes the internet's standards, and HTTP itself is defined in RFCs too. A problem has a `type` that names the kind of error, a `title`, the `status`, a `detail` about this one case, and the `instance` it happened on, and it's sent as `application/problem+json`. The first example below shows one, and the Handling Requests section builds the whole format.

## The rest of the contract

- **Auth:** who may call each endpoint, and how they prove who they are.
- **Limits:** how many requests a caller may send a minute, how big a body may be, and how many items one page of a list holds. A caller over the limit gets `429 Too Many Requests`.
- **Versions:** the `/v1` promises that what works today keeps working. A change that would break clients goes into a new version, `/v2`, while `/v1` keeps answering.
- **Docs:** a contract nobody can read doesn't help anyone. Roombook describes every endpoint in an **OpenAPI** document, a file in a standard format that tools turn into a docs page, checks, and client code. FastAPI writes it for you from your type hints, and serves a docs page at `/docs` where you can try each endpoint.

## Roombook's first endpoints

| Endpoint | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /v1/buildings` | lists the buildings |
| `GET /v1/rooms` | lists rooms, filtered by building, size, or equipment |
| `GET /v1/rooms/{roomId}` | gets one room |
| `GET /v1/rooms/{roomId}/availability?date=` | gets a room's free times on one day |
| `POST /v1/bookings` | books a room |
| `GET /v1/bookings/{id}` | gets one booking |
| `POST /v1/bookings/{id}/cancel` | cancels a booking |

The second example below shows a real API sending part of its contract in its headers.

Roombook's API is REST, but REST isn't the only style an API can take. The next lesson compares the styles you'll meet, and when each one fits.

examples.title: One error, in Problem Details
examples.prompt: Ask Roombook, on port 8000, for a room that doesn't exist.
examples.output:
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 22:55:18 GMT
server: uvicorn
content-length: 157
content-type: application/problem+json

{"type":"https://roombook.example/problems/not-found","title":"Resource not found","status":404,"detail":"Room 99 does not exist.","instance":"/v1/rooms/99"}
examples.explanation: The status line says 404. `Content-Type: application/problem+json` tells the client that the body is a problem and not a room, before it reads a word. `type` is a URL that names this kind of error and never changes, so code can check it, and `title` is a short name for that kind, for people. `status` repeats the code, for when the body travels without its headers, like in a log. `detail` explains this one case, and `instance` is the path it happened on. A booking that doesn't exist answers in exactly the same shape, with its own `detail`, so a client needs one piece of code to handle both. The header names are lowercase, as Uvicorn always writes them.

examples.title: A real API's contract, in its headers
examples.prompt: GitHub's API sends part of its contract with every answer. On a Mac or Linux, `-sI` asks for only the status line and the headers, and grep keeps four of them.
examples.output:
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
x-github-api-version-selected: 2022-11-28
x-ratelimit-limit: 60
x-ratelimit-remaining: 49
examples.explanation: `content-type` says the body is JSON. `x-github-api-version-selected` names the version of the API that answered. GitHub puts its version in a header rather than in the path, like Roombook's `/v1`, and both ways are common. `x-ratelimit-limit: 60` is how many requests you may send in an hour without signing in, and `x-ratelimit-remaining` is how many you have left, so a careful client can slow down before it ever gets a 429. The names are lowercase because GitHub answered in HTTP/2, which writes them that way, and the ones starting with `x-` are GitHub's own, not part of HTTP. Clients rely on these as much as on the JSON.

recap:
- An API is a contract: the requests a program accepts and the answers it promises for each.
- A client asks and a server answers, and either side can change inside as long as the contract holds.
- One API serves websites, phone apps, partners, scripts, and devices, and only the API touches the database.
- A server is any computer running your code: a process listening on a port, reached through DNS and an IP address.
- An API's requests and responses are HTTP with JSON bodies, and the status code is the first thing a client reads.
- An endpoint is a method and a path pattern, and a resource is a thing the API exposes, sent as a JSON representation.
- Errors, auth, limits, versions, and docs are part of the contract too.
